items.prompt: Define effective resource management in production.
items.canonical_answer: Effective resource management means producing the output customers want while wasting as little of the inputs as possible: the right quantity, the right quality and the right timing.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must relate output to the waste of inputs, not simply list resources. Naming inputs alone is not a definition.

items.prompt: A brick maker is producing well below the quantity its customers order, and its yard contains a growing pile of cracked bricks. Explain how these two signs of poor resource management could lead to falling profit for the business.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: if output falls short of the quantity customers order, the unmet demand goes elsewhere - customers who cannot get bricks when they need them are likely to buy from a rival producer, so the business loses those sales. Mechanism: the pile of cracked bricks shows inputs - clay, water, fuel and paid hours - being turned into output that cannot be sold, so the cost of every usable brick rises as the waste is spread over fewer sellable units. Consequence: revenue falls while the cost per unit rises, and the margin between price and unit cost is squeezed from both sides at once. Consequence for the stakeholders: the profit the owner earns falls, and a business whose profits keep falling may eventually fail - with the jobs of its workers at risk.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain must start from the given signs - output below orders, cracked bricks in the yard. Mechanism: award for the why or how - lost sales to rivals, waste spread over fewer saleable units. Consequence: award for the effect on profit, the owner, and for naming the stakeholder risk - workers' jobs if failure follows.

items.prompt: Palm Tree Furniture in Ongwediva makes carved wooden chairs to order. Orders have grown from 20 to 60 a month, but the workshop still finishes each chair only when the carver feels it is done, and half the finished chairs fail the owner's quality check. Explain what these figures suggest about how well Palm Tree Furniture is managing its resources, and what the owner should do first.
items.canonical_answer: The context suggests resources are badly matched to demand: the business has tripled its orders to 60 a month, yet each chair still waits on one carver's discretion, so the named cause of delay is a production rhythm unchanged since 20 orders - output is unlikely to reach 60. The reasoning for the waste: half the finished chairs failing quality check means half the wood, hours and machine time put into those chairs produces nothing the business can sell, so the inputs that went in are largely wasted. What the owner should do first: fix the quality failure - because every extra chair made to a failed standard doubles the waste - by setting a standard, checking at stages of the work rather than at the end, and only then speeding the flow of work to match the 60 orders.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using this business's facts - 20 to 60 orders, half failing the quality check. Reasoning: award for the link between unchanged working practice and missed output, and between failed checks and wasted inputs. Conclusion: award a clear choice of what to fix first, with the reasoning made explicit.

items.prompt: Explain the features of managing resources effectively in production.
items.canonical_answer: Managing resources effectively has three features: the right quantity - output matches the demand customers actually place; the right quality - the product meets the standard customers expect; and minimal waste - as little as possible of the materials, hours and machine time is lost. What it includes overall is a relationship: the inputs of the operation are converted into output with the least lost on the way, because wasted input is cost without product.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - quantity, quality, minimal waste - and for what effective management includes: matching output to demand with the least input lost.

items.prompt: Define productivity.
items.canonical_answer: Productivity is output per unit of input in a given time, most often measured as output per worker.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must make productivity a ratio of output to input - output per worker or per hour. Naming total production alone is not a definition.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between production and productivity.
items.canonical_answer: Production is the total volume of output in a given time, whereas productivity is output per unit of input - usually output per worker. The boundary is the denominator: production counts units produced, productivity divides that output by the workers (or hours, or machines) that produced it. Both sides matter: taking on 20 more workers raises production while productivity stays flat or falls, so a business can produce more bricks each week while using its workforce less well. Production answers how much was made; productivity answers how well the resources made it.
marking_guidance: Boundary/difference: award for the total-versus-ratio distinction, developed with whereas, and for showing both sides on the same example - production rising while productivity falls.

items.prompt: Explain the features of production and of productivity as measures of output.
items.canonical_answer: Production has these features: it is a total volume, it counts the units made in a given time, and it says nothing about how many resources made them. Productivity has these: it is a ratio of output to input, usually output per worker in a given time, and it is the measure that shows how well resources are being used. What the two together include is a complete picture: a business can read both to see not only how much it made but whether the inputs were worth it.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the elements of each measure - total volume against output per input - and for what the two together include: quantity judged alongside resource use.

items.prompt: Define efficiency in production.
items.canonical_answer: Efficiency is the relationship between the inputs used and the output produced: production is efficient when it achieves the most output from the fewest inputs, or the required output at the lowest cost of resources.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must relate output to inputs. Saying only "producing more" is not a definition.

items.prompt: Explain why increasing efficiency benefits a business.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is cost: when the same inputs produce more output - or the same output needs fewer inputs - the cost of each unit tends to fall, because the total input cost is spread over more units. Because each unit costs less, the margin between price and unit cost widens, or the business can cut its price and try to win sales from rivals. A second reason is security: an efficient business can profitably charge less than its rivals, which protects its sales and so its survival, while the efficiency routes themselves - automation, technology, better trained workers - create capacity to meet growing demand.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the input-output cost link, because cost per unit falls as fixed input cost spreads over more units. Second reason: award for the margin or pricing consequence, and for survival against rivals.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the main ways a business can increase productivity.
items.canonical_answer: The main ways have two features in common: each raises output per unit of input, and each works by changing how the inputs are combined. Automation and technology put repetitive stages in machine hands, which work faster and more consistently than hand work and do not tire. Improved labour skills, built through training, let each worker produce more or better output in the same hours, because skill removes the errors and hesitations that waste time. What the routes include together is the fuller picture: machines add speed and consistency, trained people add judgement and flexibility, and most businesses use both.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - automation and technology on one side, improved labour skills on the other - and for what the routes include overall: changing the input mix to raise output per input.

items.canonical_answer: Inventories are the stocks of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods that a business holds to support its production and its sales.

items.prompt: A furniture workshop holds only a few days' timber at a time because its supplier delivers weekly and is sometimes late. Its most popular dining sets are often out of stock at retailers. Explain how holding inventories could lead to higher sales and more reliable production for the workshop.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: if the workshop holds a larger buffer stock of timber, then a late or missed weekly delivery no longer stops the line, because the benches can keep being made from stock while the delivery is chased. Mechanism: production runs without interruption, so the wages, rent and machine costs of the workshop buy a full week of output rather than part of one. Consequence for the business: output becomes more reliable and the cost of each unit stabilises. On the sales side the mechanism is different: if the workshop holds finished sets, retailers can restock the day the shelf empties instead of waiting weeks, so the customer who would have drifted to a rival is served - and that is what leads to higher sales. Together the two stocks protect the business at both ends: inputs for continuity, finished goods for demand.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain must start from the given situation - weekly late deliveries, retailers out of stock. Mechanism: award for the how - buffer stock keeping the line running; finished stock filling the shelf at once. Consequence: award for the effect - reliable production, higher sales, and for the business the profit that follows.

items.prompt: Tses Cool Drinks mixes flavoured ice lollies for shops across the south. Its owner has doubled her raw material orders so the storeroom is now full, but her cash book shows almost nothing left, and the extra lollies sometimes melt in heat waves before they are sold. Explain what has happened to Tses Cool Drinks' inventories and what the owner should do next.
items.canonical_answer: The context shows the cost side of stock: doubling raw material orders filled the storeroom, and the facts here show cash leaving the business - the money paid for the stock is tied up on shelves, so almost nothing remains for day-to-day needs. The reasoning about the melting lollies is that holding more finished goods raises the risk of loss through deterioration, and the business is in the south, where heat waves destroy the product it holds - so the doubled stock is at growing risk of becoming unsaleable. What the owner should do: work back from demand and shelf life - hold a buffer of raw materials sized to supplier reliability rather than doubled, and produce lollies closer to the orders, because the damage a heat wave can do makes holding finished lollies the riskiest stock of all.

Reasoning: award for the link between holding stock and cash being tied up, and between holding finished goods and deterioration risk. Conclusion: award a clear choice - size stock to demand and shelf life rather than doubling it.

items.prompt: Define lean production.
items.canonical_answer: Lean production is an approach that cuts every form of waste from the production process - wasted materials, wasted time, idle stock and unnecessary work - so that only the resources that add value remain.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must centre on eliminating waste from the process. Naming one technique such as just-in-time is not the definition of the approach.

items.prompt: Explain why lean production benefits a business.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is that waste is cost: every unit of material thrown away, hour idled and crate of buffer stock stored has to be paid for without adding anything a customer would pay for. Because lean production removes those costs - just-in-time inventory control holds almost no stock, so storage, insurance, deterioration and tied-up cash largely disappear - the cost of each unit falls and the margin widens. A second reason is quality: a process stripped of waste and buffer stock exposes a defect at once instead of burying it, so fewer faulty units leave the works, and that is why lean tends to improve quality alongside cost.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the waste-is-cost link, because removing waste removes its cost from every unit. Second reason: award for the quality consequence - defects exposed early - and the techniques that carry it.

items.prompt: Explain the features of just-in-time inventory control and of Kaizen as lean techniques.
items.canonical_answer: Just-in-time has these features: materials arrive from suppliers only as the production line needs them; finished goods are made only as orders arrive; and inventories sit close to zero, so the costs of holding stock largely disappear. Kaizen has these: improvement is continuous and in small steps; the suggestions come from the workers themselves, who see the waste nearest; and the changes need little investment, so a stream of small corrections adds up. What the two include together is the lean approach working at two points - stock policy and the work itself.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the elements of each technique - timing of deliveries and near-zero stock for just-in-time, worker-suggested small improvements for Kaizen - and for what the pair includes as parts of one approach.

items.prompt: Define flow production.
items.canonical_answer: Flow production is a method in which the product moves continuously along a line of stages, each performing one operation, so it suits a single standardised product made in very large volumes.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must include continuous movement along stages and standardised high-volume output. Describing any large production is not a definition.

items.prompt: A sauce maker supplies one standard recipe in 2-litre bottles to supermarket chains across the region. It currently resets its kettles between every small batch. Explain how moving to flow production could lead to lower unit costs for this business.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: if the sauce moves continuously through the stages - cooking, bottling, capping, labelling - with no resets, then the line stops spending paid time on changeovers between small batches. Mechanism: the machines keep running on one standardised recipe, so each stage produces without the pauses that resetting kettles caused, and output per hour rises; the huge set-up cost of a flow line is then spread over every bottle it makes rather than over small runs. Consequence: the cost per bottle falls, so the business earns a wider margin at the same price, or can cut price to the supermarkets and defend the contract. The fit is what makes it work here: one standardised product in large volumes is exactly what flow production is for.
marking_guidance: Condition: the chain must start from the given situation - one standardised recipe, small batches with resets today. Mechanism: award for the how - continuous stages ending resets, set-up cost spread over high volume. Consequence: award for the effect on the business - unit cost down, margin wider or price defensible.

items.prompt: Otjiwa Jozi Knitwear makes school jerseys in eight school colours and four size groups, and a chain of school-wear shops has asked it to add a ninth colour for one season. Explain whether batch production is the right method for this order of work, and what the changeover would involve.
items.canonical_answer: The context fits batch: the product comes in varieties of one design - eight colours and four size groups - which is exactly what batch production serves, because the same machines make each variety and the line is reset between runs. The reasoning about the ninth colour: adding it for one season means one more reset cycle rather than a new production method, so the changeover involves re-dyeing, re-threading and re-setting the machines for the colour run, with the line producing nothing while it is reset - which is why batch runs need to be large enough to be worth the change. Conclusion: batch remains the right method here; the seasonal order is met by scheduling the ninth colour as another run, provided the run is long enough to justify its reset time.

items.prompt: Explain the features of job, batch and flow production.
items.canonical_answer: Job production has these features: one item at a time; made to the customer's own specification; and one worker or team carries the work from start to finish. Batch production has these: a group of identical items made in one run; the line or machines reset between batches; and it suits products made in varieties of the same design. Flow production has these: the product moves continuously along a line of stages; each stage performs one operation; and it suits one standardised product in very large volumes. What the three include as a set is a range from fully custom work at one end to fully standardised volume at the other.
marking_guidance: Features: award for the elements of each method - one-off custom work for job, identical runs with resets for batch, continuous single-product line for flow - and for what the set includes: a cost-versus-flexibility range.

items.prompt: Mariental Coachworks is the only business in the south that builds and repairs farm trailers. Its hand-built repairs are respected, and it also makes a standard 2-tonne tipper trailer that two farm-supply chains want to stock in bulk. The owner can afford to equip one line, not two. Consider whether Mariental Coachworks should recommend flow production for the tipper trailer.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: flow production for the standard tipper is the right recommendation, with the repair work kept as job production on the existing hand skills - one line equipped for flow, the other carried on as before. Context: the facts that decide it are the chains wanting bulk quantities of one standardised 2-tonne design, which is the demand shape flow production exists for, while the repair work is one-off and customer-specific by its nature. Criterion: what decides the choice is the order pattern - a single standard product in large volumes against varied one-off jobs. Counterargument: the case against is real - the flow line would need heavy investment, it cannot turn to repair work, and the business would depend on the two chains continuing to buy, because a flow line that stops has cost money whether or not it runs. Condition: the recommendation depends on the chains' orders being firm and lasting - if either chain pulls out, the flow line would run below the volume that pays for it, and the business would wish it had kept the flexibility of batch.

items.prompt: Define computer-aided manufacture.
items.canonical_answer: Computer-aided manufacture is the use of computers to control the machines that make a product, with the design's specification fed directly to equipment that cuts, welds or prints to it.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: the definition must name computer control of manufacturing machines. Describing design work on screen describes computer-aided design instead, which is not the same thing.

items.prompt: Explain one benefit for a manufacturer of using computers in design and manufacturing.
items.canonical_answer: A developed benefit is consistency: computer-controlled machines cut and shape every unit to the same specification, so output no longer varies from worker to worker, because the specification is carried by the machine rather than by human hands. This leads to fewer faulty units and less material thrown away, so the cost of each unit falls - and because customers receive the same standard every time, the business's reputation for quality tends to grow with its sales.
marking_guidance: Developed benefit: award for the benefit stated - consistency - developed because the machine carries the specification, and leads to the consequences of lower waste, lower unit costs and a quality reputation.

items.prompt: Explain one limitation for a manufacturer of adopting new production technology.
items.canonical_answer: A developed limitation is the investment it demands: the machines, the software and the training of workers all cost money before the first unit is produced, so a small business may find its cash committed for years before the savings arrive. Because the outlay is fixed, the technology only pays if the volume and the life of the product are long enough - and if demand falls, the business is left paying for capacity it no longer uses, which leads to losses the old hand methods were far less likely to cause.
marking_guidance: Developed limitation: award for the limitation stated - heavy upfront investment - developed because the cost comes before any output, and leads to the consequence of losses if demand falls or the product's life is short.

items.prompt: Ondangwa Sheet Metal cuts brackets by hand from chalk lines, and its two most experienced cutters are due to retire next year. A supplier has quoted a CAD/CAM cutting machine that does their work in a third of the time. Explain what the retirements change about this decision, and what the owner should check before buying.
items.canonical_answer: The context sharpens the case: the business is about to lose the two workers whose skill does the cutting, so the alternative to the machine is not hand cutting as today - it is hand cutting done by whoever can be found and trained, which is slower and more wasteful still. The reasoning is that the machine's productivity gain matters more here, because the skill it replaces is leaving anyway; the retirements turn a cost question into a capability one. What the owner should check: whether the volume of brackets justifies the quoted price - the machine pays only if it runs - whether the two cutters could be retrained to operate and maintain it before they leave, and what happens when the machine breaks down, because a business with no hand skills left is fully dependent on its repair contract.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using this business's facts - hand cutting from chalk lines, two retirements next year, a third of the time. Reasoning: award for the link between the departing skill and the machine's changed role. Conclusion: award a clear choice - buy only if the volume, the retraining and the breakdown cover check out.

items.prompt: Explain the features of how technology has changed production methods.
items.canonical_answer: The change has two named features. Computer-aided design moves the design work onto the screen, so products are drawn, tested and changed before anything physical is built - and the expensive mistakes happen on a cheap screen instead of in metal. Computer-aided manufacture feeds those designs straight to machines that cut, weld or print to the specification, so the making is controlled by computer rather than by hand. What the two include together is a chain: design and manufacture now pass from screen to machine without chalk lines, templates or re-measuring in between.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - CAD in design, CAM in manufacturing - and for what the pair includes: specification passing from screen to machine, changing how the line is organised.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Otavi Bakehouse now bakes 5 000 white loaves in each run before switching its ovens to brown bread, so it has moved from batch production to flow production." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is treating flow production as batch production at a bigger size. In fact what defines batch production is the changeover: a group of identical items is made, then the machines or line are reset to make the next group. Flow production has no runs and no changeovers - one standardised product moves continuously along a line of stages, each doing one operation. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the line ever stops to change over to a different product. Otavi Bakehouse still switches its ovens from white to brown bread, so however long each run becomes, it is still batch production: the longer run spreads each reset over more loaves, but the ovens still produce nothing while they are changed over. It would be flow production if one standardised loaf moved through mixing, proving, baking and wrapping without stopping and without switching - a method that tends to suit a single product sold in very large volumes. The size of the run does not decide the method; the changeover does.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact batch production is defined by resetting the line between groups, so a bakery that still switches between white and brown bread is using batch production however long its runs are.

A 6-mark answer states what batch production is, states what flow production is, and gives the test that separates them - whether the line stops to change over - applied to the bakery's switch from white to brown bread.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Our furniture workshop in Rundu makes each table to order, so it cannot use lean production, because lean production means having an assembly line." Explain the mistake in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The mistake is confusing lean production with flow production. Flow production is a method of organising production: one standardised product moves continuously along a line of stages, and it suits very large volumes - the assembly line the learner has in mind. Lean production is not a method of that kind. It is an approach to cutting waste - wasted materials, wasted time, idle stock and unnecessary work - and it can be applied whichever production method a business uses, including job and batch production. The test that tells them apart: ask whether the statement is about how the line is organised or about removing waste from the process. The Rundu workshop uses job production because each table is made to a customer's order, and it can still work in a lean way: cutting timber to reduce offcuts, ordering wood as each order arrives instead of filling a shed with it (provided the timber supplier delivers reliably), and asking the carpenters for small improvements to their own stage of the work. An assembly line describes flow production; the lack of one says nothing about whether a business is lean.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact lean production is an approach to cutting waste that can be applied under job, batch or flow production, while flow production is one method of organising production.

A 6-mark answer states what flow production is, states what lean production is, and gives the test that separates them - organising the line against removing waste - applied to the Rundu job-production workshop.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Mondesa Hardware keeps a month's supply of cement in its yard and reorders when the pile runs low, so it uses just-in-time inventory control." Explain the error in this statement.
items.canonical_answer: The error is treating just-in-time as another name for inventory control in general. Inventory control is any policy for deciding how much stock to hold and when to reorder it; keeping a month of cement as a buffer and topping it up when it runs low is one such policy. Just-in-time is a particular lean method of inventory control in which materials arrive as they are needed and stock is kept close to zero, so the costs of holding stock - storage space, insurance, damage and cash tied up in goods - largely disappear. The test that tells them apart: ask how much stock the policy deliberately holds. Mondesa Hardware holds a month of cement on purpose, so it is controlling its inventory with a buffer stock, which is the opposite of just-in-time. If it held cement for a day or two and its supplier delivered as customers' orders came in, that would be just-in-time - a policy that works provided the supplier is reliable and near, because one late delivery would leave the yard with nothing to sell.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact just-in-time is one method of inventory control that keeps stock close to zero, while holding a month's buffer of cement is a different inventory-control policy.

A 6-mark answer states what inventory control is in general, states what just-in-time is and the condition it depends on, and gives the test that separates them - how much stock the policy deliberately holds - applied to the hardware yard.

items.prompt: A regional manager oversees three maize mills. Mill A's workforce produced 4 000 bags last month with 10 workers; Mill B produced 6 000 bags with 24 workers; Mill C produced 3 000 bags with 6 workers. Write several linked points for the manager: work out each mill's productivity, state which mill is using its resources most effectively, and give a reason for each judgement.
items.canonical_answer: The workings. Mill A: 4 000 / 10 = 400 bags per worker per month. Mill B: 6 000 / 24 = 250 bags per worker per month. Mill C: 3 000 / 6 = 500 bags per worker per month. The judgements, with reasons. Mill C leads: at 500 bags per worker it converts its resources into output most effectively, because each worker's wages are spread over the most bags, which lowers the cost of each bag. Mill B produces the most in total - 6 000 bags - but productivity of 250 shows the largest workforce being used least well, because its output per worker is half of Mill C's; total production is not evidence of good resource use. For the manager, the next question for each mill is why: Mill A's 400 could rise through training or better mill routines, and Mill B's 250 suggests either excess staff, old equipment or poor scheduling - each mill's fix differs, which is why productivity is the starting point and not the answer.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each mill's productivity worked and stated - 400, 250, 500 bags per worker. Reason: award for the because behind each judgement - input cost spread over more bags, workforce used least well. Context: award for applying the comparison to each named mill rather than in the abstract.

facts: Mill A: 4 000 bags, 10 workers
Mill B: 6 000 bags, 24 workers
Mill C: 3 000 bags, 6 workers

items.prompt: Kalahari Kettle Snacks makes dried meat snacks for retailers. It currently holds three months of packaging and meat in a warehouse costing N$4 000 a month, plus N$60 000 of stock that its bank statements show the business cannot comfortably spare. Its two main suppliers deliver reliably and are based in the same town. Using the figures, consider whether the business should move to just-in-time inventory control.
items.canonical_answer: Judgement: yes - the facts point to just-in-time, provided the supply relationships are secured. Context: the figures that matter are the N$4 000 a month of warehouse rent, which is N$48 000 a year, and the N$60 000 of cash locked in stock - money the business shows it cannot spare. Just-in-time would free most of both: the warehouse can be given up and the N$60 000 returned to day-to-day use, and lower inventory means less damage, theft and deterioration on top. Criterion: what decides it is supply reliability, because just-in-time only works if deliveries arrive as the line needs them - and here both main suppliers are in the same town and have delivered reliably. Counterargument: the case against is that the buffer stock being removed is also the business's insurance - one broken-down delivery truck now stops the line within days, and the N$4 000 rent is a known, planned cost against which a stopped line's lost sales are not; a business that has shown cash strain may also negotiate staged delivery terms more cheaply than a full leap to near-zero stock. Condition: the recommendation depends on suppliers being local and dependable - as they are here - and on arranging a one-day safety stock for any single-sourced input before the warehouse is given up.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award a clear recommendation on just-in-time for this business. Context: award for using the figures - N$4 000 a month rent, N$60 000 tied up in stock. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - supply reliability against the holding costs saved. Counterargument: award for the case against - the lost insurance of buffer stock, the risk of a stoppage. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions - supplier dependability, safety stock for single-sourced inputs.

facts: three months of stock held
warehouse rent N$4 000 a month
N$60 000 of cash tied up in stock
two main suppliers in the same town, reliable

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "Flow production is the best method for any business that wants low unit costs." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the final recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: flow production as a continuous line of stages for one standardised product in large volumes; unit cost as the total cost of production divided by the units produced. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: a flow line spreads its huge set-up cost over very many identical units and runs without changeover pauses, so the cost per unit tends to fall below what job or batch can reach - the view is right about the arithmetic. Paragraph 3, the case against: "any business" is the false step, because a business making one-off products or many varieties cannot use flow at all - a gate maker cannot flow-produce a customer's single gate, and a bakery with three recipes needs batch's resets; a flow line also needs heavy investment, cannot change its product, and stops entirely when one stage fails, so low unit costs can come with high risk. Paragraph 4, judgement and criterion: the view holds where the product is standardised and the volume is very large - the criterion is the match between the order pattern and the method, not the unit cost alone, because a low unit cost on a product nobody wants is worthless. Paragraph 5, recommendation and conditions: flow where one standard product is made in large volumes, provided the demand is stable and lasting enough to repay the line's investment; job or batch otherwise, unless the business can reach the volumes flow needs.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must state the verdict the answer would reach - flow only for standardised high-volume output. Context: the plan must use the facts of each method - set-up costs spread, resets, investment, inflexibility. Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict - the match between order pattern and method. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against the view - one-off and varied products, risk, inflexibility. Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated conditions - stable lasting demand, volume repayment of the investment.

items.prompt: Doringbult Ceramics is a five-person pottery in a small Karas town. It makes two standard dinner-plate designs that sell steadily to guesthouses, and it has just been asked by a coastal hotel group to produce 400 matching place settings to the group's own pattern, delivered over four months. The owner is the only thrower trained on the custom work. Analyse the situation and recommend how Doringbult Ceramics should organise its production.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis. The workload now has three shapes: two standard designs in steady demand - batch work, suited to runs of one design at a time with the glazes and moulds reset between runs; a one-off commissioned pattern of 400 matching sets - which is custom to the group's specification but identical within itself, so it behaves like a single long batch rather than 400 separate jobs; and a constraint, that only the owner can throw the custom pattern, which makes her the bottleneck for both the commission and the business's judgment calls. The risk in the facts: if the owner throws all 400 place settings alone, the standard plate lines - the steady income - stall behind her, and one absence stops everything. The reasoning towards a recommendation: train one of the four other workers on the custom pattern first, so the bottleneck is doubled before the deadline tightens; schedule the commission as a series of batch runs (say, sets of the same glaze fired together), which raises efficiency because a kiln fired full of identical pieces costs the same as one fired half-empty; and protect the standard lines by alternating run weeks rather than attempting flow - at five people and two kilns, flow's investment and volume are out of reach, and flow's inflexibility would end the custom work that won the commission. Judgement: a hybrid - batch at its heart, with the owner as the quality controller of the custom runs - fits this business. Criterion: what decides it is the size of the workforce against the order book, not the size of the order alone. Counterargument: the case for turning the commission down - it ties the business's scarcest resource to one customer for four months - has weight, provided the guesthouse demand alone fills the kilns; unless that is true, the commission's guaranteed volume is worth the scheduling. Condition: the recommendation depends on the second thrower training successfully before the runs begin and on the hotel group's pattern being fixed once production starts.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award a clear recommendation on how to organise the production. Context: award for using the facts - five people, two standard designs, 400 matching sets over four months, one trained thrower. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - workforce size against the order book. Counterargument: award for the case against accepting - the owner as a four-month bottleneck, the steady lines at risk. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions - the second thrower trained, the pattern fixed.

facts: five-person pottery
two standard dinner-plate designs selling steadily
commission: 400 matching place settings to the hotel group's pattern over four months
owner is the only thrower trained on custom work
